intro: Most of the Qur'an is not written as a law code. It tells stories, praises God and warns and comforts its hearers. Yet out of a few hundred verses on inheritance, contracts, marriage, crime and war, Muslim scholars built one of the world's great legal traditions. They added the example of the Prophet, the agreement of scholars and careful reasoning by analogy, and they argued with each other for centuries.

This unit follows that work from text to law and from law to public life. You will read the verses scholars treat as legal, meet the Sunni and Shia schools of law, and see how jurists reason when the text is silent. Then you will read the verses on fighting and peace, justice and rule, and the care of the earth, each with its occasion and with the ways mainstream scholars have read it.

By the end you will be able to explain how a verse becomes a ruling, why schools of law can differ on the same verse, and how scholars answer people who pull verses out of context. You will cite surah and ayah, name the reader behind each reading, and describe debates without taking a side.
bigQuestion: How do Muslim scholars move from the words of the Qur'an to rules for law, war, rule and the care of the earth, and why do they sometimes read the same verse differently?

timeline.t: Muslim tradition dates the revelation of the Qur'an to these years, including the legal verses revealed in Medina
The Treaty of Hudaybiyya, a truce between the early Muslims and the Quraysh of Mecca
Death of Ja'far al-Sadiq, whose teaching the Ja'fari (Twelver Shia) school of law follows
Death of Abu Hanifa, founder of the Hanafi school
Death of Malik ibn Anas, founder of the Maliki school and author of al-Muwatta
Death of al-Shafi'i, whose Risala set out the roots of the law (usul al-fiqh)
Death of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, founder of the Hanbali school
Death of al-Shatibi, who wrote on the objectives of the law (maqasid)
The Amman Message affirms the recognized schools of law and limits who may declare others unbelievers
The "A Common Word" letter from Muslim scholars to Christian leaders cites love of God and neighbor

words.d: the path or way; for Muslims, God's guidance for life as a whole, which scholars try to understand
Islamic jurisprudence; the human work of understanding and stating the rules of sharia
the roots of the law; the study of the sources and methods jurists use to reach rulings
the example of the Prophet Muhammad, known mainly through hadith reports
consensus; the agreement of qualified scholars, a source of law in Sunni theory
analogy; extending a ruling from a case in the texts to a new case with the same cause
independent reasoning by a qualified scholar to reach a ruling
a school of law, such as the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali or Ja'fari
the objectives of the law, often listed as protecting religion, life, mind, family and property
striving or struggle; in the Qur'an and law, effort in God's way, including but not limited to armed defense
consultation; the Qur'an praises those who settle their affairs by mutual counsel (42:38)
a successor or steward; in 2:30, the role the Qur'an gives humans on the earth

test.q: In Sunni legal theory, which four sources are most often listed as the roots of the law?
test.why: Classical Sunni usul al-fiqh, as set out by al-Shafi'i, names the Qur'an, the Sunnah, ijma (consensus) and qiyas (analogy).

test.q: What is the difference between sharia and fiqh, as many scholars describe it?
choices: Sharia is a modern word; fiqh is ancient
Sharia is only criminal law; fiqh is only worship
Sharia is God's guidance as Muslims understand it; fiqh is the human effort to state its rules
They are two names for one written code book
test.why: Scholars commonly describe fiqh as human, fallible understanding of sharia, which is why schools can differ.

test.q: Which school of law is followed by most Twelver Shia Muslims?
test.why: The Ja'fari school is named for Ja'far al-Sadiq, an Imam in Shia tradition.

test.q: Roughly how many verses of the Qur'an do scholars usually count as legal verses?
choices: A few hundred, with estimates varying
test.why: Estimates vary, often around 500, out of more than 6,000 verses; the rest of the law was reasoned from other sources.

test.q: A jurist finds no text on a new drug. She rules it forbidden because, like wine, it clouds the mind. What method is she using?
test.why: Qiyas extends a ruling to a new case that shares the same cause ('illa), here intoxication.

test.q: What does taqlid mean in Islamic law?
choices: Following the rulings of an established school or scholar
test.why: Taqlid is following established rulings; ijtihad is reaching one by one's own qualified reasoning.

test.q: Verse 2:190 tells believers to fight those who fight them. What does the same verse add?
choices: Do not begin hostilities, for God does not love aggressors
test.why: Pickthall renders 2:190 'but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors.'

test.q: How do mainstream scholars answer those who quote 9:5 alone to justify attacks today?
choices: They say the verse is not in the Qur'an
They agree it commands attacks on all people
They say it was only a poem
They read it with its occasion, the treaty-breaking at the time, and with 9:6, which orders protection for those who ask
test.why: Mainstream commentators read 9:5 within its setting and next to 9:4 and 9:6, not as a general command.

test.q: What does 8:61 tell the Prophet to do if the enemy inclines toward peace?
choices: Incline toward it as well and trust in God
test.why: Verse 8:61 (Al-Anfal) tells the Prophet to incline toward peace when the enemy does.

test.q: In 2:30, God tells the angels He will place a khalifa on the earth. How do many modern Muslim writers on the environment read this?
choices: As a verse about building mosques
As a call to human stewardship and responsibility for the earth
test.why: Many modern readers take khalifa to mean steward or trustee, with duties toward creation.

test.q: Which verse do readers often cite for shura, or consultation?
test.why: Surah Ash-Shura (42:38) praises those whose affairs are a matter of counsel among them.

test.q: What did the Amman Message (2004) set out?
choices: A new translation of the Qur'an
A ban on all recitation competitions
Recognition of the main Sunni and Shia schools and limits on declaring other Muslims unbelievers
test.why: The Amman Message, backed by hundreds of scholars, affirmed the recognized schools and restricted takfir and who may issue fatwas.

test.q: The "A Common Word" letter of 2007 was written by Muslim scholars to whom?
test.why: It was addressed to Christian leaders and built on love of God and love of neighbor.

test.q: Which idea, developed by al-Shatibi and others, asks what purposes the law serves?
test.why: Maqasid al-sharia are the objectives of the law, such as protecting life, mind, religion, family and property.

test.q: Why do hudud punishments appear more often in headlines than in court records of many historical Muslim societies?
choices: Because the Qur'an never mentions any punishment
Because all schools abolished them in 800
Because jurists set strict standards of proof and taught avoiding them in cases of doubt
Because they apply only to angels
test.why: Classical jurists required strict proof and cited a teaching to ward off hudud in cases of doubt, so historians note they were rarely carried out.

write.prompt: Does one verse settle what Islam teaches on law or war? Pick a topic from this unit. Cite two or three passages by surah:ayah (such as 2:190, 9:5-6, 8:61, 4:59 or 2:30) and name the translation. Explain what each says, its occasion if known, and how two readers or schools read it. Then argue whether one verse alone is enough.
tips: Cite each passage as surah name and surah:ayah, and name the translator.
Attribute every reading: "al-Tabari reads this as...", "the Hanafi school holds...".
Compare readings rather than judging which is true.
Use the unit's terms, such as fiqh, ijtihad, maqasid and shura, and explain each one.
